messages.subject: Dail-Madsen Model Convergence Issue
parts:
Hi All,

I hope everyone is enjoying the holidays.

I was writing for advice on running a Dail-Madsen Model. I can't get the D-M model to converge with simulated data in JAGS when the number of individuals per site, recruitment rate, and detection probability are low. 

#------------------------ The model DOES converge with these parameters

# I am running 2 independent D-M models in the code- that's why everything has a 1 or 2. 
# Later, I'd like to connect the 2 D-M models, but right now, they are completely separate
# The complete simulation code and model are at the bottom of this email

# Number of sites
M <- 199

# Number of repeated samples
T <- 10

# Average number of individuals per site
lambda1 <- 3
lambda2 <- 3

# Average recruitment rate
gamma1 <- 2
gamma2 <- 2

# Average survival rate
omega1 <- 0.9
omega2 <- 0.9

# Average detection probability
p1 <- 0.8
p2 <- 0.8

#------------------------ The model DOES NOT converges with these parameters
# Number of sites
M <- 199

# Number of repeated samples
T <- 10

# Average number of individuals per site
lambda1 <- 1
lambda2 <- 1

# Average recruitment rate
gamma1 <- 1
gamma2 <- 1

# Average survival rate
omega1 <- 0.9
omega2 <- 0.9

# Average detection probability
p1 <- 0.3
p2 <- 0.3

#---------- Things I've tried to improve convergence:

(1) Providing realistic initial values (see code below)

(2) Running the model for 1 million iterations, with a burn-in of 100,000, and thinned by 1,000 (3 chains)
#this was the output:

My Questions:

(1) Has anyone had similar experience?

(2) Any suggestions on how to make the D-M model converge?

(3) Even more confusing is that my data (which has very low counts- and likely has small parameter estimates)- fits well using unmarked. Has anyone else seen this?

Sorry for the long email! And THANK YOU for any input!!! I really appreciate your time.
Best wishes,
Grace




#------------------------------- Here is the code for the simulated data and the model
# Number of sites
M <- 199
# Number of repeated samples
T <- 10
# Average number of hosts per site
lambda1 <- 1
lambda2 <- 1

# Average recruitment rate
gamma1 <- 1
gamma2 <- 1

# Average survival rate
omega1 <- 0.9
omega2 <- 0.9

# Average detection probability
p1 <- 0.3
p2 <- 0.3

# Days
days <- matrix(1, nrow = M, ncol = T)
  
# Data matrix + true number of hosts
y1 <- N1 <- matrix(NA, M, T)
y2 <- N2 <- matrix(NA, M, T)

# Survival + recruitment matrix
S1 <- G1 <- matrix(NA, M, T-1)
S2 <- G2 <- matrix(NA, M, T-1)

# First year= poisson process
N1[,1] <- rpois(M, lambda1)
N2[,1] <- rpois(M, lambda2)

# Second + years; survival + recruitment = abundance
for(t in 1:(T-1)) {
  S1[,t] <- rbinom(M, N1[,t], omega1^days[,t])
  S2[,t] <- rbinom(M, N2[,t], omega2^days[,t])
  # Discrete probability distribution describing the number of sucesses in a sequence of independent events, each with a probability p of sucess
  G1[,t] <- rpois(M, gamma1 * days[,t])
  G2[,t] <- rpois(M, gamma2 * days[,t])
  # Discrete probability distribution describing the probability of a given number of events occurring in a fixed time interval if the events have an average rate + are idendentent of the time since last event
  N1[,t+1] <- S1[,t] + G1[,t]
  N2[,t+1] <- S2[,t] + G2[,t]
  # Total abundance[next year] = survivors [last sampling] + gains[since last sampling]
}

y1[] <- rbinom(M*T, N1, p1)
y2[] <- rbinom(M*T, N2, p2)

sink("model.txt")
cat("
model{

#------------ Priors    

    # Initial abundance
    lambda1 ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
    lambda2 ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
    
    # Immigration rates
    gamma1 ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
    gamma2 ~ dgamma(0.001, 0.001)
    
    # Annual survivorship
    omega1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    omega2 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    
    # Detection probability
    p1 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    p2 ~ dunif(0, 1)
    
#------------ Likelihood model   

for(j in 1:nSites){
    
# Year 1
    
    N[j, 1, 1] ~ dpois(lambda1)
    N[j, 1, 2] ~ dpois(lambda2)
    
# Specify the model for years 2 through nYears
    
    for(t in 2:nReps){
    
# Estimate Survivorship
    
    S[j, t-1, 1] ~ dbin(omega1^days[j,t], N[j, t-1, 1])
    S[j, t-1, 2] ~ dbin(omega2^days[j,t], N[j, t-1, 2])
    
# Estimate recruitment
    G[j, t-1, 1] ~ dpois(gamma1 * days[j,t])
    G[j, t-1, 2] ~ dpois(gamma2 * days[j,t])
    
# Sum to get total N at location j in year t
    
    N[j, t, 1] <- S[j, t-1, 1] + G[j, t-1, 1]  
    N[j, t, 2] <- S[j, t-1, 2] + G[j, t-1, 2]  
    
    } #ts
    
 } # js

for(j in 1:nSites){
  for(t in 1:nReps){

    n[j, t, 1] ~ dbin(p1, N[j, t, 1])
    n[j, t, 2] ~ dbin(p2, N[j, t, 2])

  }
}
    
} 
    
    
    ", fill = TRUE)
sink()

#--------------------------- MCMC settings
ni <- 1000000
nb <- 100000
nt <- 1000
nc <- 3


#--------------------------- Bundle the data

y <- Ni <- array(NA, dim = c(M, T, 2))

y[,,1] <- y1
y[,,2] <- y2

win.data <- list(nSites = M, nReps = T, 
                 n = y, days = days)

#--------------------------- Initial values

Si <- Gi <- array(NA, dim = c(M, T-1, 2))

Ni[,,1] <- y1+1
Ni[,,2] <- y2+1

Si[] <- 1
Gi <- Ni[,-1,] - Si

Ni[ ,-1, ] <- NA


inits <- function(){
  list(
    omega1 = 0.9, 
    omega2 = 0.9, 
    p1 = 0.3, 
    p2 = 0.3, 
    gamma1 = 1,
    gamma2 = 1,
    lambda1 = 1,
    lambda2 = 1,
    N = Ni,
    S = Si,
    G = Gi
  )
}

#--------------------------- Parameters to monitor

params <- c("lambda1", "lambda2", 
            "omega1","omega2", 
            "p1","p2", 
            "gamma1", "gamma2")


#--------------------------- Run the model
library("jagsUI")

output2 <- jags(win.data, inits, params, "model.txt", 
                n.chains = nc, n.thin = nt, n.iter = ni, 
                n.burnin = nb, parallel = TRUE)

summary(output2)

messages.author: 527d9b3ec7deff2d
messages.subject: Re: Dail-Madsen Model Convergence Issue
parts:
Hi Grace,

What does your unmarked output look like?  Most folks find these models to be pretty unstable, particularly with low detection probabilities, small population sizes, and no secondary sampling replication.  With p=0.3 and lambda=1 there is very little information in those data, particularly for estimating both omega and gamma.  You might have better luck using a formulation where only a single dynamics parameter, the finite rate of increase, is estimated (as described in the unmarked pcountOpen help file).  I have not had much success with the DM model in JAGS, but I haven't worked with simulated data.

Hi Daniel,

Thanks for the reply!

To test some ideas out, I fitted some models in unmarked using "disease status" simply as a covariate, with the counts for the two classes "stacked". i.e., I fit a model like:

 ~ status, ~ status, ~status, ~status

 and various simplifications for the 4 parameters.   

 I fit this model to a data set with K = 4 sample occasions for one season (sampling occasions separated by a week or so, lets say).  NO REPLICATION.

 So the full model has lambda, omega, gamma, p, all depending on status -- 8 total parameters seems to converge but the SE is huge for a couple of the parameters. I guess it makes sense maybe some of them are poorly identified.  
 
 So I fit a simpler model with gammaUninfected = gammaInfected (any simplification seems to work better)..

Hi Grace,

What does your unmarked output look like?  Most folks find these models to be pretty unstable, particularly with low detection probabilities, small population sizes, and no secondary sampling replication.  With p=0.3 and lambda=1 there is very little information in those data, particularly for estimating both omega and gamma.  You might have better luck using a formulation where only a single dynamics parameter, the finite rate of increase, is estimated (as described in the unmarked pcountOpen help file).  I have not had much success with the DM model in JAGS, but I haven't worked with simulated data.

hi Dan,
 I can answer that since I did the unmarked analysis for Grace.  Here is a model selection table which shows the results of fitting a bunch of models with "disease status" as a class variable and having parameters which are either constant or dependent on disease status.  The model that is directly equivalent to the model she gave in JAGS is model 7 in the table which is specified in unmarked like this (status2 is a binary variable of disease status): 
(m6.4 <- pcountOpen(~status2, ~status2, ~status2, ~status2, umf4, K=100)) 
The table below indicates that at least 1 model has some instability issues , possibly a structural non-identifiability problem due to too many parameters (the full model has 8 total dynamics parameters and for T=4 time periods which is what I fit here that seems like a stretch -- but note: the simpler models appear stable, see below, and I used her JAGS code to try to fit those simpler models and obtain the same nonsense results in JAGS).

On Tue, Dec 29, 2015 at 9:40 AM, Daniel Linden <danl...@gmail.com> wrote:

Hi Grace,

What does your unmarked output look like?  Most folks find these models to be pretty unstable, particularly with low detection probabilities, small population sizes, and no secondary sampling replication.  With p=0.3 and lambda=1 there is very little information in those data, particularly for estimating both omega and gamma.  You might have better luck using a formulation where only a single dynamics parameter, the finite rate of increase, is estimated (as described in the unmarked pcountOpen help file).  I have not had much success with the DM model in JAGS, but I haven't worked with simulated data.
--
